body.text: budget request: 30 more simulations asked, 30 granted; the budget is now 45 (ceiling 150)
body.why: The first 12 simulations identify the UDP-loss threshold and rank TCP variants near the threshold. I need additional simulations to sweep weightUdp finely, queuePkts, duration, and seeds for the best variant(s) while enforcing udp_loss_frac <= 0.01.

body.text: The UDP loss threshold is close to the UDP demand share (about 0.30). With TcpCubic and default queue, weightUdp=0.29 should cause measurable UDP loss above 1%, while weightUdp=0.31 should keep UDP loss at or below 1%.
body.observations: E0 shows the default run (weightUdp=0.5, queuePkts=100, TcpCubic, duration=10, seed=1) has udp_goodput_bps=300003200, tcp_goodput_bps=668633114, udp_loss_frac=0.0, drops_band0=0, drops_band1=92, tcp_retrans=92, link_util=1.0. Thus UDP is already delivered without loss at the default weight, and TCP is using most of the remaining link capacity. The key question is how low weightUdp can be made while keeping udp_loss_frac <= 0.01, and which TCP variant/queue setting best exploits the remaining capacity.

body.text: When weightUdp is below UDP demand, TCP obtains a larger effective share because dropped UDP traffic does not occupy the link; therefore TcpCubic TCP goodput should be higher at weightUdp=0.29 than at weightUdp=0.31.
TcpBbr should be at least as good as TcpCubic for TCP goodput at a UDP-safe weight, because it can estimate and use the available bandwidth without relying on loss.
TcpVegas, being delay-based and less aggressive, should achieve lower TCP goodput than TcpCubic at the same UDP-safe weight.
